About: F = BIL sin θ — the force that defines the ampere

Source

Topic
Magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor
Simulation
A straight conductor rotating within a uniform horizontal magnetic field
Concept
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is F = B I L sin θ: only the component of the current perpendicular to the field counts.
Serves
NCERT Class 12 magnetism; the operational definition of the ampere; foundation for motors and moving-coil meters.
Inquiry
Rotate the wire from perpendicular toward parallel: does the force fall to a small minimum, or drop to exactly zero?
Misconception
“A current in a magnetic field always feels a force.” It does not — a current along the field lines feels nothing at all.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Set the stage

Blue lines are the field; the amber bar is the current-carrying wire; θ is the angle between them, now 90°. The green arrow is the force F — straight up, out of the plane they lie in. Imagine rotating the wire until it lies along the field (θ → 0°). What happens to F?

2 · Two angles, one force

Rotate the wire with the angle slider (θ): the force shrinks as θ falls, and at θ = 0° it is exactly zero. Now compare θ = 30° with θ = 150°.

3 · Check the claim

With θ = 0°, try turning the current or field strength up to their maximum. Does anything happen to the force?

4 · The rule

This is the standard result: F = B I L sin θ, with F perpendicular to both I and B — out of the plane they define. It is the force a motor runs on, the force a moving-coil meter balances against a spring, and the force that once defined the ampere itself.

All three controls are open. The wire's lift out of the plane and the green arrow are both drawn proportional to F.

The Physics

F = BIL sin θ — The Force That Defines the Ampere · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A straight wire carries a steady current through a uniform magnetic field, and you turn the wire to any angle. The sim shows the magnetic force on the wire as a green arrow and as a number.

What you'll learn

  • How the force on the wire depends on the angle between the current and the field.
  • How the force depends on the current and on the field strength.
  • Which way the force points, compared with the wire and the field.
Top view of the field (blue) and the wire (amber). θ is the angle from the field to the current.

What's on screen

  • Field lines (blue) run left to right, labelled Field B.
  • Wire (amber) with a current arrow, labelled Current I, and a θ arc.
  • Force arrow (green) from the wire's midpoint, labelled Force F. The wire is drawn lifted off its dashed outline by the force.
  • Readouts panel: the force F and the largest force this current and field could give.
See itTurn the wire to θ = 60° with the opening current and field. Watch for: the θ arc between the wire and the blue lines, and the green arrow rising from the wire.

03

Only the part of the wire across the field counts

Split the wire's length L into two pieces. One piece, L cos θ, runs along the field. The other, L sin θ, runs across it. The force comes only from the piece across the field, so

F = B I L sin θ
F is in newtons when B is in tesla, I in amperes and L in metres.
Only L sin θ crosses the field lines.

At the opening values, B I L = 0.60 × 6.0 × 0.50 = 1.80 N, and F is 1.80 N × sin θ:

θ0°30°60°90°120°150°180°
sin θ00.5000.86610.8660.5000
F (N)0.0000.9001.5591.8001.5590.9000.000
See itRotate the wire from θ = 90° down to 0°. Watch for: F falling from 1.800 N to 0.000 N as the green arrow shrinks to nothing.
04

Supplementary angles give the same force

Two angles that add up to 180° have the same sine, because sin (180° − θ) = sin θ. So the wire at 30° and the wire at 150° feel forces of equal size.

  • At 30° the current has a component along the field, in the same direction as B. At 150° that component points against B.
  • The two wires are mirror images across the line perpendicular to the field, so each has the same piece L sin θ = 0.25 m across the field.
  • With B = 0.60 T and I = 6.0 A, both give F = 0.60 × 6.0 × 0.25 = 0.900 N.

Only the length across the field matters. Whether the rest of the wire leans with the field or against it makes no difference to the size of F.

See itSet θ = 30°, then jump to θ = 150°. Watch for: F reading 0.900 N both times, with the wire leaning the other way.
05

Current and field scale the force, but cannot rescue it along the field

At a fixed angle, F is proportional to I and to B. At θ = 90°, with B = 0.60 T, I = 3.0 A gives 0.900 N, I = 6.0 A gives 1.800 N and I = 10 A gives 3.000 N. With I = 6.0 A, halving B to 0.30 T halves F to 0.900 N.

The readout Largest possible force is B I L, the value F would reach if the wire were turned across the field. It is 5.000 N at the top of both sliders.

At θ = 0° or 180°, sin θ = 0, so F = 0 whatever B and I are. Zero times any number is still zero. The wire has no piece across the field for B and I to act on.

See itHold θ = 0° and raise I to 10 A and B to 1.00 T. Watch for: the largest possible force climbing to 5.000 N while F stays at 0.000 N.
06

The force points at right angles to the wire and the field

The vector form is F = I L × B, where L points along the current. A cross product is perpendicular to both of its factors, so F is perpendicular to the plane that contains the wire and the field lines.

The opening picture, drawn as the sim draws it: current toward you, field to the right, force up.

Right-hand rule: point the fingers along the current, curl them toward the field, and the thumb gives the force. In the sim the current runs toward you and the field to the right, so F points up out of the page, and the wire is drawn lifted off its dashed outline by an amount that follows F.

See itTurn the wire to θ = 60°. Watch for: the wire lifted off its dashed outline, with the green arrow rising from its midpoint.
07

Where it matters

  • Electric motors. The sides of a coil carry current through a magnetic field, and the force on each side turns the coil.
  • Moving-coil meters. The force on the coil's wires is balanced by a spring, so the pointer's turn measures the current.
  • The old ampere. Two long parallel wires 1 m apart, each carrying 1 A, attract with 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length. Until 2019 this force defined the ampere.
Go deeper: where F = B I L sin θ comes from

A wire of cross-section A with n charge carriers per volume, each of charge q drifting at speed vd, carries I = nAqvd. Each carrier feels a force q vd B sin θ. A length L holds nAL carriers, so the total is nAL × q vd B sin θ = B I L sin θ.

08

Summary

In one line. The magnetic force on a wire is set by the angle between the wire and the field, together with the current and the field strength.

Key points

  • F = B I L sin θ, where θ is the angle between the current and the field.
  • The largest force is B I L, reached at θ = 90°. F = 0 at θ = 0° and 180°.
  • θ and 180° − θ give the same F.
  • F is perpendicular to both the current and the field: F = I L × B.

Common mix-ups

  • "A current in a magnetic field always feels a force." A current along the field lines feels none.
  • "Past 90° the force reverses." sin θ stays positive up to 180°, so F keeps pointing the same way and only shrinks.
  • "The force pushes the wire along the field." It pushes at right angles to both the wire and the field.

Things to try on your own

  • At θ = 90° and B = 0.60 T, find the current that gives F as close to 1 N as the slider allows.
  • With I = 10 A and B = 1.00 T, find the two angles that give F = 2.500 N.
  • Compare F with the largest possible force at θ = 45°, then at θ = 135°.
